select.title: First queries
select.summary: Meet tables, rows and columns, and read data from a table with your first SELECT queries.
select.lesson.0: A **database** stores data in **tables**. A table looks like a spreadsheet: each **row** is one record, and each **column** is one property of it. You talk to a database in **SQL**, the Structured Query Language. Almost every database understands SQL. This course runs it in SQLite.
select.lesson.1: This course uses a small table called `books`. The code below creates it: `CREATE TABLE` makes an empty table with six columns, and `INSERT INTO` adds seven rows. You learn both commands in the last world. For now, read the code as a description of the data. Every query in this course runs on this table.
select.lesson.4: `SELECT` reads data from a table. `SELECT * FROM books;` means: show all columns of the table `books`. The `*` stands for **all columns**. The answer of the database is again a table.
select.lesson.6: The price of `The War of the Worlds` is empty: the table has no price for this book. A missing value is called `NULL`. You learn how to work with it in world 4.
select.lesson.8: Most of the time you need only some columns. Write their names after `SELECT`, separated by commas. The result shows the columns in the order you write them.
select.lesson.10: Line breaks and extra spaces do not matter in SQL, so you can split a long query over several lines. The **semicolon** `;` marks the end of a statement. Keywords like `SELECT` and `FROM` are not case-sensitive, so `select` works too. Most people write keywords in capital letters, so they stand out from the names of tables and columns.
select.lesson.12: A name that does not exist is an error. `SELECT name FROM books;` fails with the message `no such column: name`, because the table has no column called `name`.
select.lesson.13: Without sorting, a database may return the rows in any order. SQLite returns them here in the order they were added. In world 3 you learn how to sort the result.
select.card.0: A table has rows (records) and columns (properties)
select.card.2: `SELECT title, year FROM books;` shows two columns
select-1.prompt: What does the `*` mean in `SELECT * FROM books;`?
select-1.options.1: all rows that are not empty
select-1.explain: After `SELECT`, the `*` stands for all columns of the table.
select-2.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
select-2.explain: The query has no filter, so it returns one row for each of the 7 books.
select-3.prompt: Complete the query so it shows all columns of the table `books`.
select-3.explain: `FROM` names the table that the data comes from: `SELECT * FROM books;`.
select-4.prompt: Build a query that shows the title and the genre of every book.
select-4.explain: List the columns after `SELECT`, separated by a comma, then name the table after `FROM`.
select-5.statement: `select title from books;` is a valid query.
select-5.explain: Keywords are not case-sensitive. `select` and `SELECT` mean the same thing.
select-6.explain: The last column before `FROM` must not end with a comma. Write `price` without the comma.
select-7.prompt: Which columns does the result have, and in which order?
select-7.explain: The result shows the columns in the order you list them after `SELECT`.
select-8.prompt: How many columns does the result have?
select-9.prompt: Match the part of the query with its job.
select-10.prompt: Put the lines in order to get a query that shows the title and the price of every book.
select-10.explain: `SELECT` comes first, then the columns separated by commas, and `FROM` with the table name comes last.
select-11.statement: Without sorting, SQL guarantees that the rows come back in the order they were added.
select-11.explain: SQL does not guarantee an order unless you sort. SQLite often keeps the order of the table, but other databases may not.
select-12.prompt: Which query shows only the titles of the books?
select-12.explain: The column comes after `SELECT` and the table after `FROM`. `*` would show all columns.
where.title: Filtering rows
where.summary: Keep only the rows you need with WHERE, comparisons, AND, OR, NOT, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE.
where.lesson.0: `WHERE` comes after `FROM` and keeps only the rows that match a **condition**. Here the condition is `year > 1850`: the database checks it for every row and shows only the books published after 1850.
where.lesson.2: Text values go in **single quotes**: `'horror'`. Numbers have no quotes. To compare, SQL uses `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Note that SQL uses a single `=` to compare.
where.lesson.4: Many databases, SQLite included, also accept `!=` for not equal, but `<>` is the standard. Always use single quotes for text: in standard SQL, double quotes are for names of tables and columns.
where.lesson.6: `AND` keeps a row only when both conditions are true. `OR` keeps a row when at least one of them is true. `NOT` turns a condition around: `NOT year > 1850` is the same as `year <= 1850`.
where.lesson.8: `AND` is evaluated before `OR`, like `*` before `+` in mathematics. `genre = 'horror' OR genre = 'novel' AND year < 1850` means `genre = 'horror' OR (genre = 'novel' AND year < 1850)`. Use parentheses to make your meaning clear: `(genre = 'horror' OR genre = 'novel') AND year < 1850`.
where.lesson.9: `BETWEEN 1815 AND 1818` keeps values from 1815 to 1818, **including** both ends. `IN` checks a list of values: `genre IN ('novel', 'horror')` is shorter than two conditions with `OR`. `NOT IN` keeps all other values.
where.lesson.12: `LIKE` compares text with a **pattern**. In the pattern, `%` stands for any number of characters (also none), and `_` stands for exactly one character. `'The%'` matches every title that starts with `The`. In SQLite, `LIKE` ignores the difference between upper and lower case letters; in PostgreSQL, it does not.
where.card.1: Text in single quotes: `genre = 'horror'`; not equal: `<>`
where.card.2: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`; use parentheses when you mix `AND` and `OR`
where-1.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
where-1.explain: Three books are older than 1820: `Emma` (1815), `Persuasion` (1817) and `Frankenstein` (1818).
where-2.prompt: Which operator means "not equal" in standard SQL?
where-2.explain: `<>` is the standard operator for not equal. Many databases also accept `!=`.
where-3.prompt: Complete the query so it shows the novels.
where-3.explain: Text values need single quotes. Without quotes, SQL reads `novel` as the name of a column, and there is no such column.
where-4.prompt: Build a query that shows the titles of the horror books.
where-4.explain: `WHERE` comes after `FROM`, and the text value `'horror'` needs single quotes.
where-5.statement: `year BETWEEN 1815 AND 1818` also matches books from 1815 and from 1818.
where-5.explain: `BETWEEN` includes both ends of the range.
where-6.prompt: Which titles does this query return?
where-6.explain: `AND` is evaluated first: the query keeps all horror books, plus novels after 1850. There are no novels after 1850, so only the two horror books remain.
where-7.prompt: This query should show the books from 1815 to 1818. Which line has the bug?
where-7.explain: `BETWEEN` always works with `AND`: write `WHERE year BETWEEN 1815 AND 1818;`.
where-8.explain: `_` stands for exactly one character, so `'_mma'` matches a four-letter title that ends with `mma`.
where-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
where-9.pairs.2: one of the values in a list
where-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: show the books from 1851 to 1897 that are not horror books.
where-10.explain: `WHERE` comes after `FROM`. The second condition is joined to the first one with `AND`.
where-11.statement: In SQLite, `WHERE title LIKE 'the%'` also finds `The Time Machine`.
where-11.explain: In SQLite, `LIKE` ignores upper and lower case for English letters. In PostgreSQL, `LIKE` is case-sensitive.
where-12.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
where-12.explain: Without novels and sci-fi, three books are left. Of these, `Dracula` (1897) and `Moby Dick` (1851) are newer than 1850.
sorting.title: Sorting and limiting
sorting.summary: Sort results with ORDER BY, keep the first rows with LIMIT, remove duplicates and rename columns with AS.
sorting.lesson.0: `ORDER BY` sorts the result by a column. It comes after `FROM` and `WHERE`. By default, it sorts in **ascending** order (`ASC`): small numbers first, and text from A to Z.
sorting.lesson.2: Add `DESC` after the column to sort in **descending** order: large numbers first, and text from Z to A.
sorting.lesson.4: You can sort by several columns, separated by commas. The database sorts by the first column. Rows with the same value there are sorted by the second column.
sorting.lesson.7: `LIMIT 3` keeps only the first three rows of the result. Together with `ORDER BY`, it answers questions like "which are the three newest books?". `LIMIT` is not part of standard SQL, but SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL all support it. The standard form is `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY`.
sorting.lesson.9: `SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result. Here every genre appears only once, even though most genres have two books.
sorting.lesson.11: `AS` gives a column a new name in the result. This new name is called an **alias**. You can also use the alias in `ORDER BY`. The table itself does not change.
sorting.lesson.13: The parts of a query always come in this order: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`.
sorting.card.0: `ORDER BY year` sorts from small to large (`ASC`)
sorting.card.1: `ORDER BY year DESC` sorts from large to small
sorting.card.4: `title AS book` renames a column in the result
sorting-1.explain: Sorted by year, the oldest book comes first. That is `Emma` from 1815, and `LIMIT 1` keeps only this row.
sorting-2.prompt: Which keyword sorts from the largest to the smallest value?
sorting-3.prompt: Complete the query so it shows only the two newest books.
sorting-3.explain: `LIMIT 2` keeps the first two rows of the sorted result.
sorting-4.prompt: Build a query that shows every genre once, sorted from A to Z.
sorting-4.explain: `DISTINCT` comes right after `SELECT`, and `ORDER BY` comes at the end.
sorting-5.statement: `ORDER BY price` without `ASC` or `DESC` sorts from the smallest to the largest price.
sorting-6.prompt: Which title is in the first row?
sorting-6.explain: `sci-fi` comes last in the alphabet, so it comes first with `DESC`. Within `sci-fi`, the titles are sorted from A to Z, and `Ti` comes before `Wa`.
sorting-7.explain: The keyword is `ORDER BY`. Write `ORDER BY year DESC`.
sorting-8.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
sorting-8.explain: There are seven books, but only five different values in `author_id`: the values `1` and `4` appear twice.
sorting-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
sorting-9.pairs.4: gives a column a new name
sorting-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: show the newest novel, with the column name `book`.
sorting-11.explain: `LIMIT` is not in the SQL standard, but SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL support it. The standard form is `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`.
sorting-12.explain: The horror books are `Dracula` and `Frankenstein`. Sorted from Z to A, `Frankenstein` comes first.
functions.title: Calculations and functions
functions.summary: Calculate with columns, change text with functions and handle missing values with NULL and IS NULL.
functions.lesson.0: `SELECT` can calculate. You can use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` with columns and numbers. The result is a new column in the result, and `AS` gives it a name.
functions.lesson.2: You can also calculate without a table, as below; this works in SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL. Be careful when you divide two whole numbers: SQLite and PostgreSQL give a whole number and drop the rest, so `7 / 2` is `3`. Write one number with a decimal point, like `7 / 2.0`, to get `3.5`.
functions.lesson.5: A **function** takes values in parentheses and gives back a result. `ROUND(price, 1)` rounds the price to one decimal place. Without the second value, `ROUND` rounds to a whole number. In SQLite the result still has `.0` at the end.
functions.lesson.7: `UPPER` changes text to capital letters, `LOWER` to small letters, and `LENGTH` counts the characters. The operator `||` joins texts together. It is standard SQL and works in SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL uses the function `CONCAT` instead.
functions.lesson.10: `NULL` means **no value**: the value is missing or unknown. `NULL` is not `0` and not an empty text. Every calculation with `NULL` gives `NULL`. A comparison with `NULL` is never true, so `price = NULL` finds nothing. To find missing values, use `IS NULL`, and for existing values, `IS NOT NULL`.
functions.lesson.13: `COALESCE(price, 0)` gives the price, or `0` when the price is `NULL`. It is standard SQL and works in all common databases.
functions.card.0: `price * 2 AS doubled` calculates a new column
functions-1.explain: The book with `id` 2 is `Dracula`, and `LENGTH` counts its 7 characters.
functions-2.explain: Both numbers are whole numbers, so SQLite drops the rest: `10 / 4` is `2`. With `10 / 4.0` you get `2.5`.
functions-3.prompt: Which condition finds the books without a price?
functions-3.explain: A comparison with `NULL` is never true. Only `IS NULL` finds missing values.
functions-4.prompt: Complete the query so it shows only the books that have a price.
functions-4.explain: `IS NOT NULL` keeps the rows where the value exists.
functions-5.explain: Every calculation with `NULL` gives `NULL`, because the value is unknown.
functions-6.explain: `ROUND` with `1` keeps one decimal place. The digit after it is `5`, so the number is rounded up to `11.8`.
functions-7.prompt: Build a query that shows every title in capital letters, with the column name `big`.
functions-7.explain: `UPPER` changes the text to capital letters, and `AS` names the new column.
functions-8.prompt: This query should show the books without a price. Which line has the bug?
functions-8.explain: `price = NULL` is never true, so the query returns nothing. Write `WHERE price IS NULL;`.
functions-9.prompt: Match the code with what it does.
functions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: show each title with its price plus 20 percent, for books that have a price.
functions-10.explain: The columns come after `SELECT`, separated by a comma. `FROM` and then `WHERE` follow.
functions-11.explain: `||` joins the title, the text `'-'` and the genre of the book with `id` 1 into one text.
functions-12.statement: This query also returns `The War of the Worlds`, which has no price.
functions-12.explain: Comparisons with `NULL` are never true, so the row with the missing price matches neither condition.
aggregates.title: Counting and totals
aggregates.summary: Summarize many rows into one value with the aggregate functions COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.
aggregates.lesson.0: An **aggregate function** combines the values of many rows into one value. The result has only one row. `COUNT(*)` counts the rows.
aggregates.lesson.2: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows. `COUNT(price)` counts only the rows where `price` is not `NULL`. One book has no price, so the two numbers are different.
aggregates.lesson.4: `SUM` adds up the values, `MIN` finds the smallest and `MAX` the largest. Like `COUNT(price)`, they skip `NULL` values.
aggregates.lesson.6: `AVG` calculates the average. The result often has many decimal places, so it is common to round it. It also skips `NULL`: the average is the sum of the six prices divided by six, not by seven.
aggregates.lesson.8: `WHERE` filters the rows **before** they are counted. This query counts only the horror books and finds the oldest year among them.
aggregates.lesson.10: `MIN` and `MAX` also work with text: they use alphabetical order. `COUNT(DISTINCT genre)` counts how many **different** values a column has.
aggregates.lesson.12: Do not mix aggregates and normal columns: `SELECT title, MAX(price) FROM books;` is an error in most databases, because the database does not know which title to show next to the one maximum. SQLite allows it, but you should not rely on it. The next world shows the right way with `GROUP BY`.
aggregates.card.0: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(price)` counts values that are not `NULL`
aggregates.card.3: `WHERE` filters the rows before the aggregate
aggregates-1.explain: Two books have the genre `sci-fi`: `The Time Machine` and `The War of the Worlds`.
aggregates-2.explain: `MAX` finds the largest year. The newest book is `The War of the Worlds` from 1898.
aggregates-4.explain: `COUNT(price)` counts only the values that are not `NULL`. One of the seven books has no price.
aggregates-5.prompt: Complete the query so it shows the total price of all novels.
aggregates-5.explain: `SUM` adds up the values. `COUNT` would count the rows, and `MAX` would find the largest price.
aggregates-6.explain: Aggregate functions skip `NULL`. The average uses only the prices that exist.
aggregates-7.prompt: Build a query that shows the lowest price, with the column name `cheapest`.
aggregates-7.explain: `MIN` finds the smallest value, and `AS` names the result column.
aggregates-8.prompt: This query should show the price of the most expensive book. Which line has the bug?
aggregates-8.explain: `MIN` finds the smallest value. For the most expensive book, write `MAX(price) AS most_expensive`.
aggregates-9.prompt: Match the function with its result.
aggregates-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: count the books from before 1850 and show the oldest year.
aggregates-10.explain: The aggregates come after `SELECT`, separated by a comma. `WHERE` comes after `FROM` and filters the rows first.
aggregates-11.prompt: What does this query return? Write it as SQLite shows it.
aggregates-11.explain: The two novels are from 1815 and 1817, so the average is 1816. `AVG` returns a decimal number, so SQLite shows `1816.0`.
aggregates-12.statement: This query returns exactly one row.
aggregates-12.explain: Without `GROUP BY`, an aggregate function combines all matching rows into one row.
grouping.title: Grouping
grouping.summary: Calculate aggregates for each group of rows with GROUP BY, and filter the groups with HAVING.
grouping.lesson.0: `GROUP BY genre` puts all rows with the same genre into one **group**. An aggregate function then works on each group separately. The result has one row per group.
grouping.lesson.2: Without `ORDER BY`, the order of the groups is not guaranteed. Sort the result when the order matters.
grouping.lesson.3: You can calculate several aggregates for each group. Here you see the oldest year and the average price of every genre. The average for `sci-fi` uses only one price, because the other one is `NULL`.
grouping.lesson.5: Every column in `SELECT` must either be in `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate function. `SELECT genre, title, COUNT(*) FROM books GROUP BY genre;` is an error in most databases, because a group has many titles. SQLite does not report this error, but the result is not useful.
grouping.lesson.6: You can group by any column. This query counts the books of each author and sorts by the number of books first.
grouping.lesson.9: `WHERE` filters rows **before** they are grouped, so it cannot use aggregates. `HAVING` filters groups **after** grouping, so it can: `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` keeps only the groups with more than one row.
grouping.lesson.11: You can use `WHERE` and `HAVING` in the same query. Here `WHERE` first removes the books from 1890 and later. Then `GROUP BY` makes the groups, and `HAVING` keeps the genres with more than one of the remaining books.
grouping.lesson.13: The full order of a query is: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`.
grouping.card.0: `GROUP BY genre` makes one row per genre
grouping.card.1: `SELECT genre, COUNT(*) FROM books GROUP BY genre;`
grouping-1.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
grouping-1.explain: There are four different genres: `adventure`, `horror`, `novel` and `sci-fi`. Each group becomes one row.
grouping-2.prompt: Which clause filters groups with an aggregate function like `COUNT(*)`?
grouping-2.explain: `HAVING` works after grouping, so it can use aggregates. `WHERE` works on single rows before grouping.
grouping-3.prompt: Complete the query so it counts the books of each genre.
grouping-3.explain: `GROUP BY genre` makes one group for each genre, and `COUNT(*)` counts the rows of each group.
grouping-4.prompt: Which genre is missing from the result?
grouping-4.explain: `adventure` has only one book (`Moby Dick`), so `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2` removes this group.
grouping-5.statement: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` keeps only the groups with more than one row.
grouping-5.explain: `WHERE` runs before grouping and cannot use aggregates. Use `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
grouping-6.prompt: Build a query that shows the newest year of each genre.
grouping-6.explain: The grouped column and the aggregate come after `SELECT`, and `GROUP BY` comes after `FROM`.
grouping-7.explain: Authors 1 and 4 have two books each. Sorted from large to small, `4` comes first, and `LIMIT 1` keeps it.
grouping-8.prompt: This query should show the genres with an average price above 7. Which line has the bug?
grouping-8.explain: Groups are filtered with `HAVING`, not `WHERE`. Write `HAVING AVG(price) > 7`.
grouping-9.prompt: Match the clause with its job.
grouping-9.pairs.0: puts rows with equal values together
grouping-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: for books after 1850, show the genres with more than one book.
grouping-11.statement: A query with `GROUP BY genre` returns one row for each different genre.
grouping-11.explain: `GROUP BY` puts all rows with the same value into one group, and every group becomes one row.
grouping-12.prompt: What number does this query show for `horror`?
grouping-12.explain: The horror books cost `7.5` and `6.25`, so the sum for this group is `13.75`.
joins.title: Joining tables
joins.summary: Add a second table for the authors and combine rows from both tables with INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and ON.
joins.lesson.0: Data is often split over several tables, so nothing is stored twice. The column `author_id` in `books` contains a number. This number is the `id` of a row in a second table, `authors`. From this world on, the database has both tables.
joins.lesson.4: `JOIN` combines the rows of two tables. After `ON` you write the condition that says which rows belong together: `books.author_id = authors.id`. Both tables have a column `id`, so you write the table name and a dot in front of the column name.
joins.lesson.6: Long table names make a query hard to read. Give each table a short alias with `AS`: after `FROM books AS b` you can write `b.title`. `JOIN` without a word in front means `INNER JOIN`. You can use `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` as usual.
joins.lesson.8: `INNER JOIN` keeps only the rows that have a partner in the other table. Jules Verne has no book in `books`, so he never appears in an inner join.
joins.lesson.10: `LEFT JOIN` keeps **every** row of the left table, which is the table after `FROM`. When a row has no partner, the columns of the other table are `NULL`. Now Jules Verne appears, with an empty title.
joins.lesson.12: Joins work together with `GROUP BY`. `COUNT(b.id)` counts only the rows with a book, so Jules Verne gets `0`. Grouping by `a.id` keeps two authors with the same name apart.
joins.card.0: `FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id`
joins.card.1: `INNER JOIN` (or `JOIN`) keeps only rows with a partner
joins.card.2: `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table; missing values are `NULL`
joins.card.3: `FROM books AS b` lets you write `b.title`
joins-1.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
joins-1.explain: Jane Austen has two books in the table: `Emma` and `Persuasion`.
joins-2.prompt: What does the condition after `ON` describe?
joins-2.options.0: which rows of the two tables belong together
joins-2.options.3: the name of a new table
joins-2.explain: The `ON` condition connects the rows, here a book with its author.
joins-3.prompt: Complete the query so it shows each book with its author.
joins-3.explain: The join condition always comes after `ON`.
joins-4.prompt: How many rows does this query return?
joins-4.explain: All 7 books have an author, and `LEFT JOIN` adds one more row for Jules Verne, who has no book.
joins-5.statement: With `INNER JOIN`, an author without books still appears in the result.
joins-5.explain: `INNER JOIN` keeps only rows with a partner. Use `LEFT JOIN` to keep every author.
joins-6.prompt: Build a query that shows each title with the name of its author.
joins-6.explain: `JOIN` names the second table, and `ON` gives the condition that connects the rows.
joins-7.prompt: This query should list every author, also authors without books. Which line has the bug?
joins-7.explain: `INNER JOIN` drops authors without books. Write `LEFT JOIN books AS b`.
joins-8.explain: `Dracula` has the `author_id` 2. In `authors`, the row with `id` 2 is Bram Stoker from Ireland.
joins-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
joins-9.pairs.0: only rows with a partner in both tables
joins-9.pairs.1: every row of the left table
joins-9.pairs.3: the column title of the table with the alias b
joins-10.prompt: Put the lines in order: show each book with its author, sorted by title.
joins-10.explain: The first table comes after `FROM`, the second after `JOIN`, then `ON` with the condition, and `ORDER BY` at the end.
joins-11.explain: `LEFT JOIN` keeps every author. For an author without a book, `b.id` is `NULL`, and only Jules Verne has no book.
joins-12.statement: This query returns 3 rows, one for each author from the UK.
joins-12.explain: The join makes one row per book. The three authors from the UK have five books, so the query returns 5 rows.
changing.title: Changing data and tables
changing.summary: Add, change and delete rows with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and create tables with PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL.
changing.lesson.0: So far you have only read data. `INSERT INTO` adds a new row. After the table name, list the columns in parentheses, and after `VALUES`, the values in the same order. Every example in this world starts again from the original tables.
changing.lesson.2: The columns you leave out get `NULL`. You can add several rows at once: separate them with commas after `VALUES`, like the course did when it created the `books` table.
changing.lesson.5: `UPDATE` changes existing rows. `SET` says which column gets which new value, and `WHERE` says which rows change. The new value can be a calculation, like `price + 1`.
changing.lesson.7: Without `WHERE`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` change **every row** of the table. Before you run them, test the condition with a `SELECT` that uses the same `WHERE`.
changing.lesson.11: `CREATE TABLE` creates a table. For each column you write a name and a type: `INTEGER` for whole numbers, `REAL` for decimal numbers and `TEXT` for text. `PRIMARY KEY` marks the column that identifies every row, so its values must be different. `NOT NULL` means the column must always have a value. In SQLite, an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` gets the next number automatically when you leave it out; other databases use words like `AUTO_INCREMENT` or `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` for this.
changing.lesson.13: The rules protect your data. If you insert a member without a name, the database refuses with the error `NOT NULL constraint failed: members.name`. If you insert a second row with the same `id`, the error is `UNIQUE constraint failed: members.id`.
changing.card.4: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, `name TEXT NOT NULL`
changing-1.explain: The book with `id` 3 costs `6.25`. The `UPDATE` adds `1`, so the new price is `7.25`.
changing-2.explain: The two horror books are deleted, so 5 of the 7 books are left.
changing-3.prompt: Which statement adds a new row to a table?
changing-3.explain: `INSERT INTO` adds rows. `UPDATE` changes existing rows, and `CREATE TABLE` creates a new table.
changing-4.prompt: Complete the statement so it changes the price of the book with `id` 1.
changing-4.explain: `UPDATE` uses `SET` to give a column its new value.
